Real-world events are now getting priced in incredibly fast in proxy markets like oil, Treasury yields, stocks, crypto, etc.

The recent oil moves tied to Saudi Arabia halting several oil operations are a good example.

I tracked how the moves played out in @loafmarkets’ Ras Tanura market:

1. Two days ago, attacks halted Saudi energy operations and pushed oil close to $100 per barrel.

2. As it happened, Ras Tanura (the world’s largest oil export terminal) jumped 52.1% in market price. An hour later, it was up 113.2%.

3. Then, when oil crossed $100 per barrel, the market rose another 31.7%.

You can see the connection pretty clearly. When the oil backdrop changes, this market reprices fast.

Some people are saying that the bull case for prediction markets is to let people trade events without basis risk, but I'm not sure that I agree it applies to ALL events.

I’m honestly amazed at the breadth & efficiency of markets we can trade nowadays.

After the $LAPTOP dumperino, I thought it would be a good idea to make a guide on how to research a token before you ape in.

Verify the token

• Get the contract address from the project's official website.
• Cross-check the address through its official social account.
• Match the full address and network before buying.
• Remember that anyone can copy a name, ticker or logo.

Check who holds the supply

• Check the biggest balances on the blockchain explorer.
• Use @bubblemaps to investigate links between wallets.
• Identify exchange, treasury, airdrop and liquidity wallets.
• Don't assume connected wallets belong to the same person.

Read the tokenomics

• Compare circulating supply with total and maximum supply.
• Check team allocations, early investor prices and unlocks.
• Verify how vesting works and who can change it.
• Confirm completed burns instead of relying on promises.

Check whether you can exit

• Compare available liquidity with the displayed market cap.
• Preview the price impact of selling your intended position.
• Check who can withdraw liquidity and when locks expire.
• Check successful sells and whether restrictions can change.

Look beyond the volume

• Compare trading volume with unique traders and liquidity.
• Investigate repetitive trades involving connected wallets.
• Confirm actual sales before calling exchange deposits dumping.
• Treat launch price spikes cautiously in thin markets.

Check the contract

• Check minting powers, blacklists and adjustable trading taxes.
• Look for transfer restrictions and contract upgrade powers.
• Identify who controls those permissions and changes.
• Read the audit's scope, unresolved findings and risks.

Research the team and the pitch

• Check the team's previous projects and delivery record.
• Confirm partnerships through the other company's channels.
• Understand what rights or benefits the token provides.
• Ask what could sustain demand after the hype fades.

I know it’s a lot, but TBH, you can give this checklist and the contract address to an LLM as a starting point. Ask it to link its sources and flag anything it couldn’t verify, then check the evidence yourself before putting money in.

Crypto projects have done ~$640M in token buybacks this year alone. Almost 90% came from Hyperliquid and Pumpfun.

Both have different buyback models:

→ @HyperliquidX: 99% of fees are routed into HYPE buybacks.

→ @Pumpfun: 50% of launchpad/PumpSwap revenue goes toward buying back PUMP.

The difference is that Hyperliquid has a stronger mechanism.

It generates more revenue and uses 99% of eligible trading fees for HYPE buybacks, while Pumpfun uses 50% of launchpad + PumpSwap revenue.

That strength comes from execution, product strength, user alignment, and trust in the team.

So IMO, buybacks work best as an amplifier. They can strengthen value accrual, but they can’t create the trust or premium the market assigns to a protocol.

Treat buybacks as support for the main thesis, not the main thesis itself.

AI competition is shifting toward what happens after pretraining.

Pretraining remains the most compute-intensive stage of model development. Chinese labs faced tighter compute constraints, so they pushed more capability gains into post-training through reinforcement learning, distillation and better training data.

DeepSeek-R1 showed that models could learn to reason by combining GRPO with rewards that were simple to verify. Because GRPO avoids using a separate model to score every answer, the training process is simpler and cheaper. 

ByteDance, Qwen and MiniMax then adapted the approach to reduce repetitive answers, improve training stability and make better use of feedback. GRPO became the starting point for a broader post-training toolkit.

The same post-training push is now extending beyond short reasoning problems. Kimi K3 breaks long agentic episodes into resumable chunks and rewards models for staying within compute budgets. Where outcomes can be checked directly, verifiable environments can replace costly human preference labels.

Distillation can then transfer reasoning capabilities from a large model to smaller models capable of running on phones, vehicles and robots. On-policy distillation goes further by having the student generate its own attempts and learn from token-level feedback rather than copying fixed answers.

Together, these advances are changing the compute and data mix. More post-training compute goes toward generating rollouts, executing environments and verifying outcomes. Generic training text becomes easier to replace, while novel real-world data and high-quality verifiable environments become more valuable.

You may had twisted ankle that was poorely recovered in the past, or maybe you carry your wallet in one backpocket of your jeans and sit a little bit unevenly for years or whatever else, your muscles learned to overcompensate around it and now it all causes a dysbalance and problems elsewhere  

Good luck!
